title: Mock 9
desc: 10 new vignettes from sub-topics different from Mock 8, plus 1 Ethics vignette

vignettes.body:
Lena Voss is valuing Hartwell Corporation common shares using a free cash flow approach. Voss gathered information about Hartwell from several sources. She begins her analysis by determining free cash flow to the firm (FCFF) and free cash flow to equity (FCFE) for the 2012 fiscal year, using the financial statements in Exhibits 1 and 2. Hartwell's fiscal year ends 31 December.

Exhibit 1
Hartwell Corporation Selected Financial Data ($ millions, except per share amounts)
# For Year Ending 31 December | 2012
Revenues | $6,102
Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) | 1,262
Depreciation expense | 231
Operating income | 1,031
Interest expense | 172
Pretax income | 859
Income tax (32%) | 275
Net income | $584
Number of outstanding shares (millions) | 395
2012 earnings per share | $1.48
2012 dividends paid (millions) | 142
2012 dividends per share | 0.36
2012 fixed capital investment (millions) | 502
Cost of equity | 11.5%
Weighted average cost of capital (WACC) | 8.5%

Exhibit 2
Hartwell Corporation Consolidated Balance Sheets ($ millions)
#   | 2012 | 2011
Cash and cash equivalents | $28 | $19
Accounts receivable | 398 | 404
Inventories | 655 | 601
Other current assets | 129 | 117
Total current assets | $1,210 | $1,141
Current liabilities | $2,640 | $2,545
Long-term debt | 2,105 | 2,305
Common stockholders' equity | 1,008 | 566
Total liabilities and stockholders' equity | $5,753 | $5,416

Voss plans to perform two different valuations of Hartwell, which she calls the "base case" valuation and the "alternative" valuation. Critical assumptions for each are given in the following lists.

Base case valuation

2013 FCFF will be $520 million.
Beyond 2013, FCFF will grow in perpetuity at 3.5% annually.
The market value and book value of Hartwell's long-term debt are approximately equal.

Alternative valuation

2013 earnings per share (EPS) will be $1.65.
EPS will grow forever at 5% annually.
For 2013 and beyond: Net capital expenditures (fixed capital expenditures minus depreciation) will be 35% of EPS. Investments in working capital will be 15% of EPS. Of future investments, 65% will be financed with equity and 35% will be financed with debt.

Greta Lindqvist, Voss's supervisor, reviews Hartwell's valuations. Specifically, Lindqvist makes the following three statements:

Statement 1: Because the company's capital structure seems unstable, the FCFE valuation approach is superior to the FCFF valuation approach.
Statement 2: If there is a change in control at Hartwell, the discounted dividend valuation approach would be superior to a free cash flow valuation approach.
Statement 3: The free cash flow valuation approach is superior to the discounted dividend valuation approach because the company's dividends have been substantially different from its FCFE.

questions.q: Hartwell's FCFF ($ millions) for 2012 is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. It uses the tax rate instead of (1 − tax rate) on interest.
B. Incorrect. It ignores the working capital investment.
C. Correct. Working capital (current assets excluding cash − current liabilities) went from −1,423 to −1,458, so WCInv = −35 (an inflow). FCFF = 584 + 231 + 172 × (1 − 0.32) − 502 − (−35) = 465.

hl: free cash flow to the firm (FCFF)
hint.rule: FCFF = NI + NCC + Int(1 − t) − FCInv − WCInv; working capital excludes cash.

questions.q: Using Voss's base case valuation assumptions and the FCFF valuation approach, the year-end 2012 value per share of Hartwell common stock is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. It discounts at the cost of equity instead of the WACC.
B. Correct. Firm value = 520 ÷ (0.085 − 0.035) = 10,400. Equity = 10,400 − 2,105 (debt) = 8,295. Per share = 8,295 ÷ 395 = $21.00.
C. Incorrect. It does not deduct the debt.

hl: FCFF will grow in perpetuity at 3.5% annually
hint.rule: FCFF value = FCFF1 ÷ (WACC − g); subtract debt for equity, divide by shares.

questions.q: Using Voss's alternative valuation assumptions and the FCFE valuation approach, the year-end 2012 value per share of Hartwell's common stock is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. It is the FCFF-style calculation: 1.65 − 0.5775 − 0.2475 = 0.825 ÷ 0.065.
B. Correct. FCFE1 = EPS − (1 − DR) × net capex − (1 − DR) × WCInv = 1.65 − 0.65 × 0.5775 − 0.65 × 0.2475 = 1.11375. Value = 1.11375 ÷ (0.115 − 0.05) = $17.13.
C. Incorrect. It grows FCFE1 again by (1 + g).

hl: EPS will grow forever at 5% annually
Of future investments, 65% will be financed with equity and 35% will be financed with debt
hint.rule: FCFE = EPS − (1 − DR)(net capex + WCInv); value = FCFE1 ÷ (r − g).

questions.q: Which of Lindqvist's three statements pertaining to Hartwell's valuation is the most accurate? Statement:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. FCFF, not FCFE, is preferred when the capital structure is unstable or changing.
B. Incorrect. With a change in control, the new owner has discretion over free cash flow and can change the dividend, so a free cash flow approach is superior to a dividend approach.
C. Correct. FCFE or FCFF is preferred to the dividend approach when dividends differ significantly from the capacity to pay them (and when control may change).

hint.rule: Unstable capital structure → FCFF; dividends unrelated to FCFE or change of control → free cash flow, not DDM.

vignettes.body:
Leon Fischer is a fund manager with Summit Asset Partners, a fixed-income asset management firm. He actively manages his fund's holdings, duration, and yield curve exposure.

Fischer's fund currently has a large position in two option-free and default-risk-free zero-coupon bonds. The first bond has a 1-year maturity and the other bond has a 10-year maturity. Fischer's view is that the spot curve one year from today will reflect the current forward curve. Interest rate information for option-free and default-risk-free zero-coupon bonds is contained in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1
Maturity (years) | 1 | 2 | 3
Spot rate | 2.50% | 3.40% | 4.30%
1-year forward rate | f0,1 = 2.50% | f1,1 = 4.31% | f2,1 = 6.12%

Fischer next focuses his attention on the short end of the yield curve. He observes the US Treasury bill rate, the overnight indexed swap rate (OIS), and the secured overnight transactions market reference rate (MRR). He collects the current rate and spread information in Exhibit 2 and uses it to calculate the 3-month TED spread.

Exhibit 2
# 3-Month US Treasury Bill Rate | 3-Month OIS Rate | 3-Month MRR – 3-Month OIS Spread
7 bps | 9 bps | 12 bps

Later in the day, Fischer meets with another analyst to discuss the current fixed-income environment. This second analyst believes fixed-income markets are about to enter a period of high uncertainty. This analyst also expects a flight to quality and a bullish flattening of the yield curve. He recommends Fischer adjust the fund's exposure through the purchase and sale of option-free default-risk-free bonds.

questions.q: If Fischer's view of spot rates one year from today is accurate, the 1-year total return of the 10-year bond will be:
options: equal to the total return of the 1-year bond.
greater than the total return of the 1-year bond.
less than the total return of the 1-year bond.
questions.why:
A. Correct. If spot rates evolve as the current forward curve implies, bonds of every maturity earn the one-year (risk-free) rate over the year.
B. Incorrect. It would be higher only if spot rates fell below those implied by the forward curve.
C. Incorrect. It would be lower only if spot rates rose above those implied by the forward curve.

hl: spot curve one year from today will reflect the current forward curve
hint.rule: Spot curve evolves as the forward curve implies → every bond earns the one-year spot rate.

questions.q: Fischer's view that the spot curve one year from today will reflect the current forward curve is most consistent with:
options: the segmented markets theory.
the liquidity preference theory.
the pure expectations theory.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Segmented markets: each maturity is priced by its own supply and demand; forward rates are not forecasts.
B. Incorrect. Liquidity preference adds a premium for longer maturities, so forward rates overstate expected future spot rates.
C. Correct. Pure expectations: forward rates are unbiased predictors of future spot rates, so the future spot curve equals today's forward curve.

hl: spot curve one year from today will reflect the current forward curve
hint.rule: Future spot = today's forward rates is the pure expectations theory.

questions.q: The 3-month TED spread that Fischer calculates should equal:
options: 5 bps.
14 bps.
19 bps.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. It subtracts the T-bill rate from the MRR–OIS spread (12 − 7).
B. Correct. 3-month MRR = OIS + (MRR − OIS spread) = 9 + 12 = 21 bps. TED spread = MRR − T-bill rate = 21 − 7 = 14 bps.
C. Incorrect. It adds the T-bill rate to the MRR–OIS spread (12 + 7).

hint.rule: TED = MRR − T-bill; MRR = OIS + (MRR − OIS spread).

questions.q: The strategy best suited to exploit the second analyst's expected changes to the current fixed-income environment is to:
options: extend duration and construct a barbell portfolio.
keep duration constant and construct a barbell portfolio.
extend duration and construct a bullet portfolio.
questions.why:
A. Correct. Flight to quality: government yields fall, so extend duration. Bullish flattening: long rates fall more than short rates, so shift from a bullet to a barbell.
B. Incorrect. Duration should be extended when yields are expected to fall.
C. Incorrect. Extending duration is right (flight to quality lowers yields) but a bullet suits a parallel shift or a steepening, not a bullish flattening.

hl: flight to quality and a bullish flattening of the yield curve
hint.rule: Yields fall (flight to quality) → extend duration; bullish flattening → barbell.

vignettes.body:
Helen Marsh is an analyst at Beacon Fund covering the real estate and energy sectors. She and her colleague are analyzing two companies that are currently held by the fund.

The first company is Mercury Corp., a publicly traded, national retail grocery store chain that has 3,100 physical stores. Mercury leases most of its grocery stores and all five of its office locations that help the company achieve its core business of operating 50,000 square foot stores in all markets of the United States. Mercury also owns the real estate (land and building) associated with 120 physical store locations. Mercury recently announced that its board of directors approved a strategic real estate plan to pursue a separation of all its owned assets. The company currently has a speculative-grade credit rating.

The separation would be achieved through a series of sale-leaseback transactions with real estate investment trusts (REITs) that specialize in owning retail properties. Under the plan, Mercury will sell its 120 owned grocery stores and lease them for 20-year terms with a combined annual rent expense of USD54 million. Mercury expects to receive cash proceeds of approximately USD1,000 million from the property sales, which will be used to retire approximately USD700 million of debt and repurchase 5 million common shares.

Mercury believes the pro forma capital structure following the transactions will enable it to receive an investment-grade credit rating. The sale-leaseback transactions value the 120 assets at an average capitalization rate of 5.40%. Based on Marsh’s colleague’s research, the 25th, 50th, and 75th percentile cap rates for sale transactions for similarly situated properties and similar lease terms in the last three years were 4.90%, 5.40%, and 5.90%, respectively.

The second company is Neptune Corp., a publicly traded US energy company. Marsh has been asked to assess the valuation of a potential spin off for this company. Neptune operates and reports three segments: Upstream, Midstream, and Downstream. In the last 12 months, the company reported the financial results shown in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1
# Segment | EBITDA (USD millions)
Upstream | 12,600
Midstream | 4,200
Downstream | 2,800
Consolidated | 19,600
Neptune is currently trading at an enterprise value of USD313,600 million, or an EV/EBITDA multiple of 16. A spin off of the Downstream segment has long been rumored because it has been under-invested in by the current management team, resulting in slower revenue growth than its peers. Marsh finds that the median Upstream, Midstream, and Downstream peers are trading at enterprise value-to-EBITDA multiples of 18, 15, and 12, respectively.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about Mercury's motivations for the strategic real estate plan is incorrect?
options: The expected change in Mercury's credit rating after the transactions will increase the firm's costs of capital.
The transactions will allow Mercury to unlock the value of its real estate assets.
The transactions will enable Mercury to sell a non-core business.
questions.why:
A. Correct. Retiring debt should improve the credit rating, which lowers (not raises) the cost of capital, so this statement is incorrect.
B. Incorrect. Sale-leasebacks unlock the value in the real estate: Mercury receives cash and records a lease liability.
C. Incorrect. Real estate ownership is not Mercury's core business (operating grocery stores), so this statement is correct.

hl: pursue a separation of all its owned assets
retire approximately USD700 million of debt
hint.rule: Less debt → better credit rating → lower cost of capital; real estate is a non-core business for a grocer.

questions.q: Which of the following statements best describes Mercury's average capitalization rate for the sale-leaseback transactions? Mercury's average capitalization rate:
options: is supported by the comparable transactions.
compares favorably to the comparable transactions.
compares unfavorably to the comparable transactions.
questions.why:
A. Correct. The average cap rate of 5.40% equals the median (50th percentile) of comparable transactions (4.90%, 5.40%, 5.90%), so it is supported.
B. Incorrect. 5.40% is not better than the median of comparable transactions.
C. Incorrect. 5.40% is not worse than the median of comparable transactions.

hint.rule: Cap rate equal to the median of comparables = supported by the market.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1 and the peer median EV/EBITDA multiples, Neptune's estimated enterprise value is closest to:
options: USD294,000 million.
USD313,600 million.
USD323,400 million.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. It uses the average of the peer multiples (15) for every segment.
B. Incorrect. USD313,600 million is Neptune's current enterprise value, not the estimate.
C. Correct. Sum of the parts: Upstream 12,600 × 18 = 226,800; Midstream 4,200 × 15 = 63,000; Downstream 2,800 × 12 = 33,600; total 323,400.

hint.rule: Sum of the parts: each segment's EBITDA × its own peer median multiple.

questions.q: A spin-off of the Downstream segment would most likely:
options: distribute shares of the Downstream business to Neptune's existing shareholders.
sell the Downstream segment to another company for cash.
sell shares of the Downstream business to new investors in a public offering, giving Neptune cash.
questions.why:
A. Correct. In a spin-off the parent distributes the shares of the subsidiary pro rata to its own shareholders; no cash is raised.
B. Incorrect. That describes a divestiture (sale) of the segment, not a spin-off.
C. Incorrect. That describes an equity carve-out, which raises cash for the parent.

hl: A spin off of the Downstream segment
hint.rule: Spin-off = shares distributed to existing shareholders, no cash; carve-out = IPO of a minority stake; divestiture = sale.

vignettes.body:
Daniel Ashworth is an equity analyst at an investment bank. He is preparing updated research reports on two companies, Zorin Incorporated and Harlan Company.
Zorin Incorporated
Ashworth indicates in his updated report that Zorin's profits are cyclical. Using the data for the past four years in Exhibit 1, he computes Zorin's normalized EPS based on the average ROE method. He determines that Year 1 through Year 4 (the most recent year) constitutes a full business cycle.
Exhibit 1
#   | Year 1 | Year 2 | Year 3 | Year 4
EPS | $2.84 | $1.96 | $0.52 | $2.31
Book value per share | $11.40 | $12.20 | $12.90 | $13.60
Harlan Company
Ashworth next reviews Harlan, which operates in a previously mature industry that now has high growth potential due to a recent technological innovation. Harlan's debt-to-equity ratio is significantly higher than the average of its competitors. Harlan spent heavily on advertising to create and maintain its brand, which is an important asset. The company is favored by many investors because its dividend payout ratio is the highest in its industry. Ashworth considers several potential metrics to use in valuing Harlan.
During the past year, Harlan's share price rose from $24.60 to $28.35 per share and the company paid an annual dividend of $1.10 per share. Over the same period, the market index rose from 488.30 to 521.90 and had an average dividend yield of 3.1%. Ashworth computes Harlan's relative strength compared to the index, which is a common technical indicator.

questions.q: Ashworth finds that Zorin's profits are cyclical. Compared with the latest reported EPS, normalized EPS is used because it:
options: uses forecast earnings, which are always available for cyclical companies.
adjusts reported earnings for the effect of share repurchases.
estimates the earnings Zorin would earn at mid-cycle, removing the effect of the business cycle.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Forecast earnings give a forward P/E; normalized earnings are an estimate of average earnings over a full cycle.
B. Incorrect. Share repurchases are not what normalizing is for.
C. Correct. Normalized EPS removes the influence of the business cycle by estimating mid-cycle earnings (here average ROE over a full cycle times current book value per share).

hint.rule: Cyclical profits → use normalized (mid-cycle) EPS, e.g. average ROE × current BVPS.

questions.q: Zorin's normalized EPS based on the average ROE method is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. $1.91 is the average EPS of Years 1 to 4.
B. Incorrect. $1.94 multiplies the average ROE (15.5%) by the AVERAGE book value per share ($12.525) instead of the current one.
C. Correct. ROE by year: 24.9%, 16.1%, 4.0% and 17.0%, average 15.5%. Normalized EPS = average ROE × current (Year 4) book value per share = 0.1550 × $13.60 = $2.11.

hl: Year 1 through Year 4 (the most recent year) constitutes a full business cycle
hint.rule: Normalized EPS = average ROE of a full cycle × CURRENT book value per share.

questions.q: Which of the following is the most appropriate metric for Ashworth to use in valuing Harlan?
options: Price to book ratio
Enterprise value to sales ratio
Dividend yield
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Book value ignores Harlan's brand, an internally generated intangible asset built by advertising that is not on the balance sheet.
B. Correct. EV/sales uses the total value of debt and equity, so it suits Harlan's high debt-to-equity ratio and diverse capital structures; sales are stable and hard to manipulate.
C. Incorrect. Dividend yield ignores capital gains, which are likely important with the industry's growth potential, and the highest payout in the industry may not be safe.

hl: debt-to-equity ratio is significantly higher than the average of its competitors
spent heavily on advertising to create and maintain its brand
hint.rule: High leverage + valuable internal brand → enterprise value to sales, not P/B or dividend yield.

questions.q: Harlan's relative strength compared to the market index over the past year is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct. Relative strength = (Harlan price ÷ index) at the end divided by the same ratio at the start = (28.35 ÷ 521.9) ÷ (24.6 ÷ 488.3) = 0.054321 ÷ 0.050379 = 1.0782. Dividends are not included.
B. Incorrect. 1.0479 compares Harlan's price return with the index's total return (price change plus the 3.1% yield); relative strength uses prices only.
C. Incorrect. 1.0885 compares total returns (adds Harlan's $1.10 dividend and the index yield); relative strength uses prices only.

hint.rule: Relative strength = (stock ÷ index) now ÷ (stock ÷ index) at the start; price only, no dividends.

vignettes.body:
Marovia, a resource-abundant West African country, has a developing economy with low capital per worker available. Although the majority of its population is impoverished, Marovia has a long history of advanced education and is committed to technological progress. President Emmanuel Kessogo recently appointed Aminata Camara, PhD, as Economic Development Secretary. He asks her to help him develop economic policies to promote growth.

Last year, Kessogo attended a summit of international leaders, where he learned that developing countries typically face several factors that affect their growth prospects, such as enforcement of substantive laws, restrictions on imports, and low rates of saving.

Kessogo believes that the Marovia economy relies too heavily on the export of natural rubber. He is convinced that significant industrial capital investment will persuade foreign direct investors that he is serious about economic development. He announces that the Marovia government will construct a large tire factory to take advantage of the country’s rubber resources. Kessogo expects that as a result of this investment, per capita productivity will rise rapidly driving rapid growth in GDP.

Camara believes that according to the classical growth theory, gains in per capita GDP are temporary because the resulting population explosion will lower per capita GDP to subsistence real wage levels. She considers endogenous growth theory to be more realistic, believing that (1) investments, such as the new tire factory, will increase the rate of per capita output growth until the steady state rate of growth is achieved; and (2) investment in research and development will boost growth even further, thus extending the abnormal growth period before diminishing marginal returns eventually set in.

questions.q: Camara's understanding of the two growth theories is most accurate with regard to:
options: classical growth theory.
endogenous growth theory.
both classical growth theory and endogenous growth theory.
questions.why:
A. Correct. Her view of classical theory is right: gains in per capita GDP are temporary because the resulting population growth pushes income back to subsistence.
B. Incorrect. Her description of endogenous theory is wrong: a steady state of growth and diminishing marginal returns are features of neoclassical theory; endogenous theory has no diminishing returns to capital (R&D, human capital).
C. Incorrect. Her understanding of endogenous growth theory is incorrect.

hl: gains in per capita GDP are temporary
steady state rate of growth is achieved
hint.rule: Classical = temporary gains (population); neoclassical = steady state, diminishing returns; endogenous = no diminishing returns.

questions.q: Which of the following factors favors economic growth?
options: Limited foreign capital and trade flows
Limited regulations in order to encourage entrepreneurial activity
Low rates of saving
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Foreign investment and trade can raise the capital stock, productivity, employment and wages.
B. Correct. Limited regulation encourages new companies, which are strongly correlated with higher productivity.
C. Incorrect. Low saving and investment limit growth.

hl: enforcement of substantive laws, restrictions on imports, and low rates of saving
hint.rule: Growth helped by savings, open trade and capital flows, entrepreneurship; hurt by import restrictions and weak law enforcement.

questions.q: According to the neoclassical growth model, when trade barriers are removed, convergence of per capita income levels between developed and developing countries should:
options: occur more slowly.
remain unaffected.
occur more quickly.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Opening up speeds up, not slows down, convergence.
B. Incorrect. Opening up affects the rate of growth and convergence.
C. Correct. With open trade and capital flows, capital moves to poorer countries and their capital-to-labor ratios rise faster, so productivity and per capita incomes converge more quickly.

hint.rule: Neoclassical + open economy: capital flows to the poor country → faster convergence.

questions.q: Opening an economy to trade and financial flows will most likely:
options: discourage domestic spending on research and development.
not impact domestic spending on research and development.
encourage domestic spending on research and development.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Open trade encourages, not discourages, R&D spending.
B. Incorrect. Open trade affects innovation by encouraging R&D and human capital spending.
C. Correct. Open trade gives access to larger markets and a greater flow of ideas, so firms invest more in R&D and human capital, raising the return on new investment and growth (though small, lagging countries can lose domestic innovation).

hl: Opening an economy to trade and financial flows
hint.rule: Open economy: larger markets and idea flow → more R&D and human capital investment.

vignettes.body:
Mariko Ishikawa works as a senior examiner for the Financial Institutions Agency (FIA), and Kenji Mori is one of the analysts who reports to her. Mori is a new hire who previously worked at an investment firm that specialized in manufacturing companies. His first two weeks at the FIA were spent in training sessions focused on the Basel III regulatory framework for banks to prepare him for his new analyst role.

At today’s weekly meeting, Ishikawa and her analysts are conducting a preliminary review of some of their assigned insurance institutions. Mori arrives early, so Ishikawa takes the opportunity to ask him to explain his understanding of the Basel III framework. Mori describes three enhancements that Basel III incorporated as part of its transition from the previous iteration:

Enhancement 1: More stringent capital requirements that prevent banks from taking on excessive financial leverage.
Enhancement 2: Increased funding stability by giving preference to interbank deposits over those from consumers.
Enhancement 3: Additional measures to ensure sufficient earnings quality, thereby strengthening banks’ regulatory capital.
The other analysts arrive, and the meeting gets underway. The group is scheduled to review an insurance company, Kitano Holdings (KH), a property and casualty insurer. Ishikawa notes that the property and casualty market has been in a “hard” phase for a few years now, and she wonders whether the results will show the beginning of a cyclical shift.

The group reviews KH’s profitability information that Mori has provided in Exhibit 1. Ishikawa asks Mori to calculate KH’s combined ratio:

Exhibit 1 Excerpts from KH’s Financial Statements
(¥ billions)
Loss expense and loss adjustment expense | 41,208
Net premiums earned | 58,420
Net premiums written | 52,130
Underwriting expense | 21,874

questions.q: Which of the enhancements Mori describes regarding the Basel III regulatory framework is most accurate?
options: Enhancement 1
Enhancement 2
Enhancement 3
questions.why:
A. Correct. After the 2008 crisis, Basel III raised the required equity funding of banks' risk-weighted assets, which prevents banks from taking on excessive financial leverage.
B. Incorrect. Basel III did increase requirements for stable funding, but consumer deposits are considered more stable than interbank deposits, so the preference is for consumer deposits.
C. Incorrect. Earnings quality was not a focus of Basel III, although its changes will likely improve earnings quality.

hint.rule: Basel III: more equity against risk-weighted assets (less leverage), stable funding from consumer deposits.

questions.q: If Ishikawa's interpretation of the current phase of the property and casualty market is correct, a cyclical shift is most likely to result in:
options: additional competitors entering the market.
capital adequacy being easier to achieve.
a tightening of underwriting standards.
questions.why:
A. Correct. In a hard market premiums, profits and underwriting standards are high; this attracts competitors that offer lower premiums, which softens the market and weakens underwriting standards.
B. Incorrect. Hard markets help insurers maintain adequate capital; capital depletes as the market softens, making capital adequacy harder to achieve.
C. Incorrect. In a hard market underwriting standards are already high; as the market softens they drop, not tighten.

hl: “hard” phase for a few years now
hint.rule: Hard market: high premiums and profits → new competitors → soft market: lower premiums, weaker underwriting standards, capital harder to maintain.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1, KH's combined ratio is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. 70.5% is only the loss ratio (41,208 ÷ 58,420).
B. Correct. Combined ratio = loss ratio + underwriting expense ratio = 41,208 ÷ 58,420 + 21,874 ÷ 52,130 = 70.5% + 42.0% = 112.5% (loss expense is divided by net premiums earned, underwriting expense by net premiums written).
C. Incorrect. 121.0% uses net premiums written for the loss ratio too (79.0% + 42.0%).

hint.rule: Combined ratio = loss & LAE ÷ net premiums earned + underwriting expense ÷ net premiums written.

questions.q: KH's combined ratio indicates that its underwriting business, before investment income, is:
options: break-even, because the combined ratio is measured on net premiums written.
profitable, because the loss ratio is below 100%.
unprofitable, because claims and expenses exceed the premiums earned.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. The combined ratio is not defined on net premiums written alone.
B. Incorrect. The loss ratio alone ignores the underwriting expense ratio; the combined ratio adds both.
C. Correct. A combined ratio above 100% means claims, loss adjustment expenses and underwriting expenses exceed the premiums, so the underwriting is a loss that investment income must cover.

hint.rule: Combined ratio > 100% = underwriting loss (covered only by investment income).

vignettes.body:
Priya Menon is a risk manager for a bank. She manages the bank’s risks using a combination of swaps and forward rate agreements (FRAs).

Menon prices a three-year MRR-based interest rate swap with annual resets using the present value factors presented in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1
Present Value Factors
# Maturity (years) | Present Value Factors
1 | 0.985222
2 | 0.964949
3 | 0.939556
Menon also uses the present value factors in Exhibit 1 to value an interest rate swap that the bank entered into one year ago as the pay-fixed (receive-floating) party. Selected data for the swap are presented in Exhibit 2. Menon notes that the current equilibrium two-year fixed swap rate is 1.80%.

Exhibit 2
Selected Data on Fixed for Floating Interest Rate Swap
Swap notional amount | $40,000,000
Original swap term | Three years, with annual resets
Fixed swap rate (since initiation) | 2.75%
One of the bank’s investments is exposed to movements in the Japanese yen, and Menon desires to hedge the currency exposure. She prices a one-year fixed-for-fixed currency swap involving yen and US dollars, with a quarterly reset. Menon uses the interest rate data presented in Exhibit 3 to price the currency swap.

Exhibit 3
Selected Japanese Interest Rate Data
# Days to Maturity | Yen Spot Interest Rates
90 | 0.08%
180 | 0.14%
270 | 0.20%
360 | 0.30%
Menon reviews current MRR data in Exhibit 4. Based on her interest rate forecast, Menon also considers whether the bank should enter into a new position in a 2 × 5 FRA.

Exhibit 4
Current MRR (Market Reference Rate)
30-day MRR | 0.78%
60-day MRR | 0.85%
90-day MRR | 0.92%
120-day MRR | 0.95%
150-day MRR | 0.98%
180-day MRR | 1.00%
210-day MRR | 1.02%
270-day MRR | 1.06%

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1, Menon should price the three-year MRR-based interest rate swap at a fixed rate closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct. Fixed swap rate = (1 − final-year PV factor) ÷ (sum of the PV factors) = (1 − 0.939556) ÷ (0.985222 + 0.964949 + 0.939556) = 0.060444 ÷ 2.889727 = 2.09%.
B. Incorrect. It leaves the final-year PV factor out of the denominator: 0.060444 ÷ (0.985222 + 0.964949) = 3.10%.
C. Incorrect. It does not divide by the sum of the PV factors: 1 − 0.939556 = 6.04%.

hl: three-year MRR-based interest rate swap with annual resets
hint.rule: Fixed swap rate = (1 − last PV factor) ÷ sum of the PV factors.

questions.q: From the bank's perspective, using data from Exhibit 1, the current value of the swap described in Exhibit 2 is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. The size is right but the sign is wrong: $741,065 would be the value to the receive-fixed party.
B. Correct. Two years remain, so the sum of the PV factors is 0.985222 + 0.964949 = 1.950171. For the receive-fixed party the value is (2.75% − 1.80%) × 1.950171 × $40,000,000 = $741,065. The bank pays fixed, and the fixed rate it pays is above today's equilibrium rate, so its value is −$741,065.
C. Incorrect. It uses all three PV factors (sum 2.889727), but only two years remain: $1,098,096.

hl: entered into one year ago as the pay-fixed (receive-floating) party
current equilibrium two-year fixed swap rate is 1.80%
hint.rule: Swap value = (old fixed rate − current fixed rate) × sum of the remaining PV factors × notional; the pay-fixed party loses when the old rate is above the current rate.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 3, Menon should determine that the annualized equilibrium fixed swap rate for Japanese yen is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. 0.0749% is the quarterly (periodic) rate, not the annualized rate.
B. Incorrect. 0.1800% is just the average of the yen spot rates, not a swap rate.
C. Correct. Yen PV factors = 1 ÷ [1 + rate × (days ÷ 360)]: 0.999800, 0.999300, 0.998502, 0.997009 (sum 3.994612). Periodic rate = (1 − 0.997009) ÷ 3.994612 = 0.0749%. Annualized = 0.0749% × (360 ÷ 90) = 0.2995%.

hl: one-year fixed-for-fixed currency swap involving yen and US dollars
hint.rule: Currency swap fixed rate for one currency: PV factors from that currency's spot rates, periodic rate = (1 − last PV) ÷ sum of PV, then multiply by 4 for quarterly resets.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 4, the fixed rate on a new 2 × 5 FRA is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. It divides by 150/360 instead of the 90-day FRA period: 0.64%.
B. Correct. FRA rate = {[1 + L150 × (150/360)] ÷ [1 + L60 × (60/360)] − 1} ÷ (90/360) = {1.004083 ÷ 1.001417 − 1} × 4 = 1.07%, using the 60-day MRR of 0.85% and the 150-day MRR of 0.98%.
C. Incorrect. It divides by 60/360 instead of the 90-day FRA period: 1.60%.

hl: a new position in a 2 × 5 FRA

vignettes.body:
Walter Dunn, CFA, is the chief financial officer for Green Valley Nurseries, one of the largest producers of flowers and bedding plants in the Western United States. Green Valley Nurseries grows its plants in three large nursery facilities located in California. Its products are sold in its company-owned retail nurseries as well as in large, home and garden "super centers". For its retail stores, Green Valley Nurseries has designed and implemented marketing plans each season that are aimed at its consumers in order to generate additional sales for certain high-margin products. To fully implement the marketing plan, additional contract salespeople are seasonally employed.
For the past several years, these marketing plans seemed to be successful, providing a significant boost in sales to those specific products highlighted by the marketing efforts. However, for the past year, revenues have been flat, even though marketing expenditures increased slightly. Dunn is concerned that the expensive seasonal marketing campaigns are simply no longer generating the desired returns, and should either be significantly modified or eliminated altogether. He proposes that the company hire additional, permanent salespeople to focus on selling Green Valley Nurseries' high-margin products all year long. The chief operating officer, David Larsen, disagrees with Dunn. He believes that although last year's results were disappointing, the marketing campaign has demonstrated impressive results for the past five years, and should be continued. His belief is that the prior years' performance can be used as a gauge for future results, and that a simple increase in the sales force will not bring about the desired results.
Dunn gathers information regarding quarterly sales revenue and marketing expenditures for the past five years. Based upon historical data, Dunn derives the following regression equation for Green Valley Nurseries (stated in millions of dollars):
Expected Sales = 9.8 + 2.1 (Marketing Expenditures) + 0.9 (# of Salespeople)
Dunn shows the equation to Larsen and tells him, "This equation shows that a $1 million increase in marketing expenditures will increase the independent variable by $2.1 million, all other factors being equal." Larsen replies, "It also appears that sales will equal $9.8 million if all independent variables are equal to zero."

questions.q: In regard to their conversation about the regression equation:
options: Dunn's statement is correct; Larsen's statement is correct.
Dunn's statement is correct; Larsen's statement is incorrect.
Dunn's statement is incorrect; Larsen's statement is correct.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Dunn says the independent variable rises by $2.1 million, but expected sales is the dependent variable, so he is wrong.
B. Incorrect. Dunn is wrong because expected sales is the dependent variable.
C. Correct. Larsen is right: 9.8 is the intercept, the expected sales (in millions) when all independent variables are zero.

hl: increase the independent variable by $2.1 million
sales will equal $9.8 million if all independent variables are equal to zero
hint.rule: Slope: change in the DEPENDENT variable per unit of the independent variable; intercept: dependent variable when all independent variables are zero.

questions.q: Dunn explains the standard error of estimate (SEE) to Larsen with three points. Point 1: If there is a strong relationship between the variables and the SEE is small, the individual estimation errors will also be small. Point 2: The SEE is the standard deviation of the differences between the estimated values for the independent variables and the actual observations for the independent variable. Point 3: Any violation of the basic assumptions of a multiple regression model is going to affect the SEE. How many of Dunn's points are most accurate?
options: 2 of Dunn's points are correct.
1 of Dunn's points is correct.
All 3 of Dunn's points are correct.
questions.why:
A. Correct. Point 2 is wrong: the SEE measures differences between estimated and actual values of the DEPENDENT variable. Points 1 and 3 are correct, so two points are correct.
B. Incorrect. Points 1 and 3 are also correct, so more than one point is correct.
C. Incorrect. Point 2 is incorrect, so not all three are correct.

hint.rule: SEE = standard deviation of the residuals (dependent variable); small SEE = strong fit; violations of assumptions affect it.

questions.q: Assuming that next year's marketing expenditures are $2,800,000 and there are six salespeople, predicted sales for Green Valley Nurseries should be:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. It leaves out the intercept: 2.1 × 2.8 + 0.9 × 6 = 11.28, i.e. $11,280,000.
B. Incorrect. It leaves out the salespeople term: 9.8 + 2.1 × 2.8 = 15.68, i.e. $15,680,000.
C. Correct. The equation is in millions of dollars: 9.8 + 2.1 × 2.8 + 0.9 × 6 = 21.08, i.e. $21,080,000.

hint.rule: Plug the values into the equation and keep the units (millions).

questions.q: Dunn wants to test whether the marketing coefficient of 2.1 is still significantly different from zero after a year of flat revenues. He should compare:
options: the R² of the regression with the SEE.
the t-statistic (the coefficient divided by its standard error) with the critical t-value.
the F-statistic of the whole regression with the critical F-value.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. R² and the SEE describe fit, they do not test a single coefficient.
B. Correct. The significance of one slope coefficient is tested with a t-test.
C. Incorrect. The F-test checks whether at least one independent variable explains a significant part of the variation, not one specific coefficient.

hint.rule: One coefficient → t-test; all coefficients together (at least one ≠ 0) → F-test.

vignettes.body:
Daniel Kwon, CFA, is an investment manager looking to diversify his portfolio by adding equity real estate investments. Kwon and his investment analyst, Elena Varga, are discussing whether they should invest in publicly traded real estate investment trusts or public real estate operating companies. Varga expresses a strong preference for investing in public REITs in taxable accounts.

Kwon schedules a meeting to discuss this matter, and for the meeting, Kwon asks Varga to gather data on two specific REITs and come prepared to explain her preference for public REITs over public REOCs. At the meeting, Kwon asks Varga,

“Why do you prefer to invest in public REITs over public REOCs for taxable accounts?”

Varga provides Kwon with an explanation for her preference of public REITs and provides Kwon with data on the two REITs shown in Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2.

The meeting concludes with Kwon directing Varga to identify the key investment characteristics along with the principal risks of each REIT and to investigate the valuation of the two REITs. Specifically, Kwon asks Varga to value REIT A using two different methodologies:

Valuation Method 1: Relative valuation using property subsector average P/AFFO multiple
Valuation Method 2: Net asset value

Exhibit 1
Select REIT Financial Information
# | REIT A | REIT B
Property subsector | Office | Storage
Estimated 12-month cash net operating income | $420,000 | $295,000
Funds from operations | $388,420 | $301,880
Cash and equivalents | $275,300 | $214,300
Accounts receivable | $188,600 | $301,700
Debt and other liabilities | $2,386,000 | $2,097,000
Non-cash rents | $31,204 | $27,015
Recurring maintenance–type capital expenditures | $72,415 | $58,430
Shares outstanding | 63,800 | 71,200

Exhibit 2
REIT A Assumptions and Average Price Multiple
Assumed cap rate | 6.5%
Property subsector average P/AFFO multiple | 16.8×

questions.q: Varga's most likely response to Kwon's question is that the type of real estate security she prefers:
options: has below-average correlations with overall stock market returns.
provides dividend income that is exempt from double taxation.
offers a high degree of operating flexibility.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. REITs do not have below-average correlation with the stock market; that is not the reason for the preference in taxable accounts.
B. Correct. REITs are tax-advantaged entities: in jurisdictions such as the United States they avoid the double taxation of income (corporate level and again on dividends), while REOCs are not typically tax-advantaged.
C. Incorrect. Operating flexibility is an advantage of REOCs, not REITs (REITs have restrictions on their activities).

hl: preference for investing in public REITs in taxable accounts
hint.rule: REIT: tax-advantaged (no double taxation); REOC: operating flexibility, no payout requirement.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2, the value per share for REIT A using valuation Method 2 is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. It leaves out cash and receivables: (6,461,538 − 2,386,000) ÷ 63,800 = $63.88.
B. Correct. NAV: operating real estate = 420,000 ÷ 0.065 = 6,461,538; plus cash and receivables 463,900; less debt and other liabilities 2,386,000 = 4,539,438; ÷ 63,800 shares = $71.15.
C. Incorrect. It does not deduct the debt and other liabilities: (6,461,538 + 463,900) ÷ 63,800 = $108.55.

hint.rule: NAV per share = (cash NOI ÷ cap rate + cash + receivables − liabilities) ÷ shares.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2, the value per share of REIT A using valuation Method 1 is closest to:
questions.why:
A. Correct. AFFO = FFO − non-cash rents − recurring maintenance-type capex = 388,420 − 31,204 − 72,415 = 284,801. AFFO per share = 284,801 ÷ 63,800 = $4.46. Value = $4.46 × 16.8 = $74.99.
B. Incorrect. It forgets to deduct the recurring maintenance-type capex: (388,420 − 31,204) ÷ 63,800 × 16.8 = $94.06.
C. Incorrect. It applies the multiple to FFO per share instead of AFFO per share: 388,420 ÷ 63,800 × 16.8 = $102.28.

hint.rule: AFFO = FFO − non-cash rents − recurring capex; value = AFFO per share × P/AFFO multiple.

questions.q: The risk factor most likely to adversely affect an investment in REIT B is:
options: new competitive facilities.
obsolescence of existing space.
tenants' sales per square foot.
questions.why:
A. Correct. REIT B is a storage REIT; entry into self-storage is easy, so overbuilding and new competing facilities are the main risk.
B. Incorrect. Obsolescence of existing space is a typical concern for office REITs.
C. Incorrect. Tenants' sales per square foot is a risk measure for retail (shopping center) REITs.

hint.rule: Match the property subsector to its main risk: storage = new competitive facilities (easy entry).

vignettes.body:
Sterling Investment Partners is a global asset management firm offering a wide variety of mutual funds to both institutional and individual investors. Victor Almeida, Sterling’s chief risk officer, is responsible for risk oversight across the firm’s many strategies, as well as communication of any risk issues to the portfolio management, compliance, and executive teams. Almeida oversees a team of six analysts who are responsible for the ongoing calculation and assessment of portfolio risk. Sterling uses a variety of methods when estimating risk, including value at risk (VaR), sensitivity risk measures, and scenario risk measures.

Joanna Whitfield just joined Sterling as a risk analyst, and Almeida is familiarizing her with how the firm measures portfolio risk. In a conversation with Whitfield, Almeida asks her what she has learned regarding the advantages of using VaR as a risk management tool. Whitfield responds, “The advantages of VaR are that it (1) provides an estimate of downside exposure during a worst-case scenario, (2) avoids subjectivity, and (3) can be used for performance evaluation.”

Later that day, Whitfield receives an email from Almeida asking her to estimate the dollar VaR at the 5% level for the firm’s developing market equity fund. Whitfield estimates VaR using the parametric method (assuming normal distribution) with the inputs in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1 Data for Developing Market Equity Fund
Portfolio value | $800 million
Daily expected return | 0.05%
Daily expected volatility | 1.10%
Almeida receives a call from Sandra Hollis, Sterling’s CEO. Hollis expresses her concern that the firm’s $600 million multi-asset fund has failed to protect investors during a recent market decline. Almeida drafts an updated risk management policy to present to the investment committee. The goal of this policy is to ensure that the fund limits the likelihood of severe downside losses for investors. The new policy reads as follows:

“The multi-asset fund has a 5-day, 1% VaR limit of $12 million and a cumulative 30-day loss limit of $18 million.”

Following the investment committee’s approval, Hollis references the updated risk management policy in her quarterly letter to investors. She states, “At Sterling, we take risk management very seriously. In response to recent investor concerns about volatility in our multi-asset fund, we have implemented a new policy. We limit fund losses to 2% of assets with a 99% level of confidence, with additional measures to limit total losses to 3% over a rolling 30-day period.”

questions.q: Whitfield's comments on the advantages of VaR are most likely correct regarding:
options: downside exposure.
subjectivity.
performance evaluation.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. VaR is not a worst-case scenario; losses can and will exceed VaR.
B. Incorrect. VaR relies on subjective inputs: the confidence level, the time horizon and the estimation method.
C. Correct. VaR can be the basis for risk adjustment of returns, which is needed in performance evaluation.

hl: can be used for performance evaluation
hint.rule: VaR: useful for risk-adjusted performance; subjective inputs; NOT a worst case.

questions.q: Using the inputs in Exhibit 1, Whitfield's estimate of VaR is most likely closest to:
options: $8.8 million.
$14.1 million.
$20.1 million.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. It multiplies the portfolio value by the daily volatility only ($800 million × 1.1%).
B. Correct. Parametric 5% VaR: 1.65 × 1.10% = 1.815%; subtract the expected return of 0.05%: 1.765%; × $800 million = about $14.1 million.
C. Incorrect. It uses the 1% z-score (2.33) instead of the 5% z-score (1.65): (2.33 × 1.10% − 0.05%) × $800 million = $20.1 million.

hint.rule: Parametric VaR = (z × volatility − expected return) × portfolio value; 5% → z = 1.65.

questions.q: A limitation of the parametric method that Whitfield used to estimate VaR is that it:
options: uses actual past returns, so it cannot capture new risks.
assumes returns are normally distributed, which fits poorly with fat tails and options.
requires a large number of random scenarios to be generated.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. Using actual past returns describes the historical simulation method.
B. Correct. The parametric method assumes a normal distribution, which understates tail risk and does not suit portfolios with options.
C. Incorrect. Generating random scenarios describes Monte Carlo simulation.

hint.rule: Parametric = normal distribution assumption (weak for fat tails and options); historical = past data; Monte Carlo = random scenarios.

questions.q: Hollis's comments to Sterling's investors are least likely accurate with regard to her:
options: use of confidence levels.
discussion of limiting losses.
implied percentage declines from dollar VaR limits.
questions.why:
A. Incorrect. A 1% VaR is appropriately a 99% level of confidence.
B. Correct. VaR is a minimum loss for a given confidence level; it does not limit losses (the loss can be the whole portfolio value), so she is wrong to say the fund limits losses.
C. Incorrect. VaR can be expressed in percentages: $12 million on $600 million is 2%, and $18 million is 3%.

hl: limit fund losses to 2% of assets with a 99% level of confidence
hint.rule: VaR = minimum loss at a confidence level, not a loss limit.
